lessons.title: Registers hold values
lessons.body: A register is a small storage location inside the CPU. eax is the low 32-bit part of rax. All examples use Intel syntax: instruction destination, source. mov copies the source without erasing it.
lessons.task: Copy the value 7 into eax. Fill the instruction mnemonic.
lessons.hint: The copy instruction is mov.
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: Choose the destination
lessons.body: The destination is written first in Intel syntax. Changing eax changes the value returned by a function returning int. ret returns to the caller; we study how calls work later.
lessons.task: Return the integer 12 by filling in the destination register.
lessons.hint: For an int result, write eax.
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: Add without losing track
lessons.body: add destination, source updates the destination with their sum. First trace the starting value, then apply the operation. These snippets are function bodies, not standalone operating-system programs.
lessons.task: Make eax equal 9 by filling the immediate value.
lessons.hint: Find the difference between 9 and 4.
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: Subtract a value
lessons.body: sub destination, source subtracts the source from the destination. The destination keeps the result. These exercises use small values that do not overflow.
lessons.task: Return 6. Fill the subtraction instruction.
lessons.hint: Use sub to subtract.
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: Copy between registers
lessons.body: mov can copy between registers of the same size. ecx and eax are both 32-bit. In this snippet ecx already contains 15; copying it must preserve that value.
lessons.task: Copy ecx into eax.
lessons.hint: The source operand is on the right.
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: Multiply by a constant
lessons.body: The three-operand imul form multiplies its second operand by the immediate third operand and stores the result in its first. This is integer multiplication.
lessons.task: Compute 3 times 6 and return it.
lessons.hint: Use the signed integer multiplication mnemonic imul.
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: Read memory, not the address
lessons.body: Square brackets mean access memory at an address. Assume rdx points to a valid 32-bit integer containing 21. mov eax, edx would copy address bits; mov eax, [rdx] reads the integer.
lessons.task: Load the integer at the address held in rdx. Fill the complete source operand, including brackets.
lessons.hint: Put square brackets around rdx.
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: Store through a pointer
lessons.body: A memory destination writes data. Assume rdx points to a writable 32-bit integer. eax is a register, while [rdx] is a memory location. The register operand tells the assembler the width.
lessons.task: Store eax into the pointed-to integer.
lessons.hint: Put the address register in brackets as the destination.
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: Compare and branch
lessons.body: cmp sets flags based on a subtraction without storing the subtraction result. je branches if equal; jne branches if unequal. A label names an instruction position. Here we supply eax=8 so you can trace the equal path.
lessons.task: Jump to equal_case when eax equals 8.
lessons.hint: je and jz are synonymous here.
lessons.template:
mov eax, 8
cmp eax, 8
[[0]] equal_case
mov eax, 0
ret
equal_case:
mov eax, 1
ret
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: Signed less-than
lessons.body: For signed integers, jl means jump if less and jge means jump if greater or equal. Unsigned comparisons use other conditions. Use signed values throughout this task.
lessons.task: Return 1 when ecx is less than 10, otherwise return 0.
lessons.hint: Use jump-if-less, jl, not the unsigned jb.
lessons.template:
cmp ecx, 10
[[0]] below_limit
mov eax, 0
ret
below_limit:
mov eax, 1
ret
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: A loop in three steps
lessons.body: A loop needs a body, an update, and a condition. dec subtracts one; jnz branches when the zero flag is clear. dec sets that flag, so the loop ends when ecx reaches zero. Trace ecx=3,2,1 and count the additions.
lessons.task: Fill the update and branch so this function returns 6.
lessons.hint: Decrease ecx by one, then repeat if it is not zero.
lessons.template:
mov eax, 0
mov ecx, 3
again:
add eax, 2
[[0]] ecx
[[1]] again
ret
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: The stack: a matched pair
lessons.body: In x86-64, push rax subtracts 8 from rsp and stores eight bytes; pop rax reads eight bytes and adds 8. Match the pair before ret, because ret needs the caller’s return address at the top of the stack.
lessons.task: Restore the saved rax after the temporary change.
lessons.hint: The matching operation for push is pop.
lessons.template:
push rax
mov eax, 99
[[0]] rax
ret
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: Call and return
lessons.body: call pushes a return address and transfers control to a function. ret consumes the saved address. This leaf helper uses no stack variables. The caller below aligns its stack for System V x64 and reserves Windows x64 shadow space.
lessons.task: Call the helper and return normally.
lessons.hint: Use call to enter a function and ret to return.
lessons.template:
sub rsp, 40
[[0]] helper
add rsp, 40
ret
helper:
mov eax, 17
[[1]]
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: Linux GCC: first argument
lessons.body: The System V x86-64 ABI used by our GCC Linux builds passes the first int argument in edi and returns int in eax. This is an ABI convention, not an instruction-set rule. Compare the equivalent C function on godbolt.org.
lessons.task: Complete int plus_two(int x) for Linux x64.
lessons.hint: The Linux x64 first int argument is in edi.
lessons.teacher: Mxy · Learn Assembly For Beginners | Introduction to Assembly | Assembly Tutorial x86-64 Architecture

lessons.title: Windows MSVC: first argument
lessons.body: Windows x64 uses ecx for the first int argument and edx for the second. int results still use eax. Do not apply this to 32-bit MSVC. In Compiler Explorer choose x64 MSVC, paste int add(int a,int b){return a+b;} and compare with x86-64 GCC.
lessons.task: Complete the Windows x64 integer addition function.
lessons.hint: Use ecx then edx; System V would use edi then esi.

lessons.title: Bridge to reverse engineering
lessons.body: Combine copying, arithmetic, and return. Start by translating the C expression to operations, then check a few inputs on paper. This is a Linux System V x64 function; the following C→Assembly course explores compiler output.

add eax, [[2]]
[[3]]

lessons.title: Read argc and argv as memory structures
lessons.body: Command-line arguments become a count and an array of pointers. argc includes the program name. argv[argc] is a null pointer; each earlier entry points to a separate zero-terminated string. Recovering argv[2] therefore requires locating the pointer array, selecting its third pointer, then following it. On ordinary x64, adjacent pointers are eight bytes apart; x86 pointers are four bytes apart. This pointer stride is different from the spacing between characters inside an argument. The source spelling of main can disappear, but the uses of its two parameters help identify it. Never read argv[2] before proving argc is at least three. Debugger command syntax is another layer: run 6 9 supplies two arguments; quotation rules determine how a string containing a space is grouped. Record both the launch command and the actual argc/argv values when reproducing behavior.
lessons.code:
Launch: ./reader 6 9
argc = 3
argv[0] -> "./reader"
argv[1] -> "6"
argv[2] -> "9"
argv[3] = NULL
walkthrough: Draw the pointer array separately from the three strings.
At main in a debug build, inspect argc, argv[1], and argv[2] with print and x/s.
Compile a guarded argv[2] accessor for GCC x86/x64 and local MSVC; compare pointer scales.
lessons.solution: argv[2] begins at offset 16 in an x64 pointer array, but that slot contains an address, not the character 9 itself. Following the stored pointer reveals the string. The count is three, not two.

lessons.title: From source to a running image: where evidence changes
lessons.body: A C source file is not an executable image. Preprocessing resolves includes, macros, and conditional compilation. Compilation lowers the resulting translation unit to assembly or intermediate machine-oriented representations. Assembly encodes instructions and produces a relocatable object. Linking combines objects and libraries, resolves symbols, and creates the executable. Loading maps that image into a process and prepares runtime dependencies. Some compilers combine stages internally, but the logical distinctions still help explain artifacts. An undefined reference at link time differs from a syntax error at compile time; a missing shared library at startup is a loading problem. Debug information and symbol tables add useful names but do not recreate every original source decision. Keep one small program and save each stage so you can observe when names, bytes, and addresses first become meaningful.
lessons.code:
# On a normal Linux C toolchain, for the casebook storage example:
gcc -E storage.c -o storage.preprocessed.c
gcc -S -O0 -masm=intel storage.c -o storage.s
gcc -c -O0 storage.c -o storage.o
gcc -g -O0 storage.c driver.c -o storage-local
# objdump -dr storage.o shows relocations in an object.
# objdump -d -M intel storage-local shows the linked image.
walkthrough: Predict why storage.o cannot be launched as the finished command-line program.
Compile storage.c without driver.c and explain the missing entry/main diagnostic on your ordinary toolchain.
Compare a relocation in the object with the corresponding reference in the linked image.
lessons.solution: A relocatable object can contain valid machine code while still needing unresolved symbols fixed by a linker. A linked image has addresses within its chosen layout; runtime relocation may still change actual virtual addresses. Each stage answers a different question.
lessons.task: Which stage normally resolves references between separately compiled objects?
lessons.hint: Use the worked example to construct your own explanation, then compare with the solution.

lessons.title: Bits, hexadecimal, and little-endian memory
lessons.body: Memory is byte-addressed. A byte contains eight bits and represents values 0–255 when unsigned. Hexadecimal groups four bits per digit, so a byte is two hex digits. In little-endian x86, the least significant byte of a multi-byte integer is at the lowest address. This describes byte order in memory, not reversed spelling of every hexadecimal value. The bytes 78 56 34 12 represent the 32-bit value 0x12345678. An instruction listing is also a sequence of bytes, but decoding instructions is different from reading one integer. Always record the width: reading eight bytes where only four belong to a variable can accidentally combine neighboring objects.

lessons.title: Widths, aliases, and zero extension
lessons.body: rax, eax, ax, and al are overlapping views of one register, not independent variables. rax is 64 bits; eax is its low 32; ax is its low 16; al is its low 8. In 64-bit mode, writing a 32-bit general-purpose register clears the upper 32 bits of the containing 64-bit register. Writing an 8- or 16-bit part generally leaves the other bits unchanged. This is why mov eax,0 can clear rax, while mov al,0 cannot. Pointers in the ordinary x64 model need 64-bit address registers; using eax for an address can truncate it. movzx explicitly zero-extends a smaller value; movsx sign-extends it. The data type and instruction width must agree.
lessons.code:
mov rax, -1
mov al, 0       ; rax = 0xffffffffffffff00
mov eax, 1      ; rax = 1
movsx eax, byte ptr [rdx]  ; sign-extend one byte
walkthrough: Track all 16 hex digits of rax after each write.

Identify which instruction extends a byte and whether the extension copies the sign bit.
lessons.solution: Writing al modifies only the lowest byte. Writing eax clears the high half of rax. A signed byte 0xFF becomes -1 after sign extension; zero extension produces 255.

lessons.hint: A 32-bit write clears the high 32 bits.

lessons.title: Flags: signed and unsigned are different questions
lessons.body: cmp a,b computes flags as if subtracting b from a but does not save the subtraction. ZF indicates a zero result. CF describes unsigned borrow for subtraction; OF describes signed overflow. je/jz test equality, which is independent of signedness. For order, signed jl tests SF != OF while unsigned jb tests CF. The same bits can represent different mathematical values depending on type. 0xFFFFFFFF is -1 as int32_t and 4294967295 as uint32_t. With that value compared to 1, signed less-than is true and unsigned below is false. A conditional branch is only meaningful with the instruction that last set its flags; an intervening add may replace cmp's flags.
lessons.code:
mov eax, -1
cmp eax, 1
jl signed_less   ; taken
; With jb here instead, the branch would not be taken.
walkthrough: Compile signed and unsigned less-than functions in Godbolt.
Find jl/setl versus jb/setb or equivalent optimized forms.
Trace equality separately from ordering; list the instruction supplying flags for every branch.
lessons.solution: Interpretation changes the order relation, not the stored bits. jg/jge/jl/jle are signed conditions; ja/jae/jb/jbe are unsigned conditions. test x,x checks zero without modifying x.
lessons.task: Which mnemonic means unsigned jump-if-below?
lessons.hint: Signed less is jl; unsigned below is jb.

lessons.title: Bitwise operations and shifts
lessons.body: and keeps bits set in both operands; or sets bits appearing in either; xor sets bits that differ. xor eax,eax is a common zeroing idiom. test performs an AND for flags without storing the result, useful for a bit mask. shl shifts left, shr shifts right with zeros, and sar shifts right replicating the sign bit. For nonnegative bounded integers these often resemble multiplication or division by powers of two, but signed division rounds toward zero while arithmetic right shift of a negative odd number rounds down on x86. Do not casually replace all signed division with sar. Compilers can add a bias before shifting to preserve C semantics.
lessons.code:
mov eax, 0x2D
and eax, 0x0F  ; eax = 13
shr eax, 1     ; eax = 6

lessons.title: Signed division and integer conversion
lessons.body: For 32-bit signed division, idiv divides the signed 64-bit dividend in edx:eax by its operand, placing quotient in eax and remainder in edx. cdq prepares edx by sign-extending eax. Clearing edx is appropriate for an unsigned nonnegative dividend with div, but is wrong for a negative signed dividend. Division by zero or a quotient that does not fit raises a processor exception. At optimization, a constant divisor may become multiplication and shifts; recover the mathematical behavior by checking multiple inputs instead of assuming a multiply means source multiplication. Casts can also produce movsx/movzx with no branch at all.

lessons.title: Addressing modes, lea, and the 32-bit bridge
lessons.body: An effective address can combine base + index*scale + displacement, where scale is 1,2,4,8. mov eax,[rdx+rcx*4] reads an int from an array. lea computes the address expression without reading memory; it is also useful for arithmetic. In 32-bit x86, use eax/esp/ebp for values, stack, and a conventional frame pointer; pointers are normally four bytes. In x64 the counterparts are rax/rsp/rbp and pointers are normally eight bytes. int remains commonly four bytes on both platforms. GCC -m32 needs 32-bit development libraries for linked C programs; if unavailable, use -m32 -S on a header-free function to study assembly without linking. MSVC requires the x86 developer prompt for 32-bit builds.

lessons.title: String instructions: copy, fill, compare, and scan
lessons.body: The processor has implicit-operand instructions for buffers. In ordinary 64-bit address-size operation, movsb copies a byte from [rsi] to [rdi]; stosb stores al at [rdi]; cmpsb compares bytes at [rsi] and [rdi]; scasb compares al with [rdi]. Address-size changes can select other index/count widths. DF controls whether the index registers advance or retreat; cld selects forward movement. rep movsb repeats for rcx bytes, reducing the count each time. repe cmpsb continues while compared bytes are equal and count remains; repne scasb continues while bytes do not match and count remains. For scasb, the updated destination index is rdi, not rsi. After a forward search finds a byte, rdi points just past it. Check the zero-count case separately because no comparison occurs then. These patterns may implement library-like operations, but a compiler can instead emit calls, scalar loops, or vector instructions.
lessons.code:
Assume valid non-overlapping 4-byte buffers and DF=0:
mov rcx, 4
rep movsb
; RSI and RDI each advance by 4; RCX becomes 0.
; x86 address-size counterparts use ESI, EDI, ECX.

lessons.title: RIP-relative addresses use the next instruction
lessons.body: In x64 a RIP-relative memory operand uses the address after the current instruction plus a signed displacement. A disassembler may display the resolved address instead of that arithmetic, hiding the distinction between encoded displacement and target location. If an instruction starts at 0x2000, occupies six bytes, and has displacement 0x30, its effective target is 0x2036. A negative displacement points backward. lea rax,[rip+disp] computes an address; mov eax,[rip+disp] reads the value at that address. Relative addressing can keep an internal reference valid when the whole image moves together. It does not mean every x64 address is relative, or that arbitrary file offsets equal virtual addresses. Verify instruction size, sign extension, and section mapping before editing a displacement.

Instruction length: 6 bytes
Signed displacement: +0x30
Target = 0x2006 + 0x30 = 0x2036

lessons.title: Process memory and the address you are actually using
lessons.body: Distinguish file layout from virtual memory. An executable contains sections and metadata on disk; the loader creates mappings with permissions and initializes state. Code is commonly mapped executable, writable globals belong to data mappings, zero-initialized static storage may occupy virtual space without equivalent stored bytes, and dynamic allocations and stacks have runtime lifetimes. These are useful patterns, not a promise of one fixed address diagram. A local value can live in a register, and constants can be merged. Two processes may use the same virtual address for unrelated memory. A debugger displays target-process addresses, while a file patcher edits byte positions in a file. Heap allocation, stack lifetime, and global storage describe ownership/lifetime as well as location. A returned pointer to a dead stack object is not made valid by still seeing old bytes there.
lessons.code:
One investigation, three coordinate systems:
file offset → image-relative location → current process VA

A stored zero-initialized global may require virtual space
without one matching initialized byte for every byte of that space.

lessons.title: Read two assembly dialects without changing the program
lessons.body: Intel and AT&T syntax are display conventions for the same instruction set. Ordinary two-operand Intel syntax places the destination first; AT&T commonly places the source first, prefixes registers with %, and marks immediates with $. Size suffixes and memory-address notation also differ. Confirm the tool’s dialect before interpreting an operand as an address or an immediate. Hexadecimal 0xNN and assembler forms ending in h are notation choices, not different Linux and Windows encodings. x86 instructions have variable length; disassembling from the wrong byte can produce plausible but unrelated instructions. In 64-bit mode the low-byte names for the extended registers are r8b through r15b, not r8l. FS and GS can still have important uses on modern systems, including thread-related state; do not assume every segment register became irrelevant in long mode.

AT&T:   movl $29, %eax
Intel:  mov eax, [rdx+rcx*4+8]
AT&T:   movl 8(%rdx,%rcx,4), %eax

lessons.title: Global, local, static: identify storage before names
lessons.body: Scope and storage duration are different. A stack local is often accessed relative to rbp or rsp; a global or static-duration object commonly appears at a fixed image-relative location. On x64, RIP-relative addressing is a frequent global access pattern. Initialized writable data often lives in .data; zero-initialized static storage often uses .bss; read-only constants may be in .rodata or .rdata. Names and sections are clues, not proof: optimizers can remove locals, keep them in registers, merge constants, and fold globals. A static local persists across calls just as a global does even though its source scope is restricted. Reconstruct lifetime from writes and repeated calls.

lessons.title: Pointers, indirection, and aliasing
lessons.body: A pointer stores an address; a pointee is the object at that address. Distinguish p, *p, and &p. A load of a pointer followed by another load can represent an extra level of indirection, a struct field, or a pointer array; use surrounding operations to decide.

lessons.title: Build a stack frame from evidence
lessons.body: In a conventional 32-bit frame, call has placed the return address at entry esp. push ebp saves the caller frame pointer; mov ebp,esp anchors the frame; sub esp,N reserves local space. The first stack argument is then often [ebp+8], while locals use negative offsets. leave is effectively mov esp,ebp followed by pop ebp, and ret consumes the return address. This is one common pattern, not a requirement: optimization may omit the frame pointer or allocate locals differently. An add esp,4 frees space; sub esp,4 reserves it because the stack grows toward lower addresses.
lessons.code:
push ebp
mov ebp, esp
sub esp, 16
mov eax, [ebp+8]
mov [ebp-4], eax
leave
ret
walkthrough: Draw saved ebp at offset 0, return address at +4, argument at +8, local at -4.
Explain every change to esp in chronological order.
Compare to a GCC x64 frame; note eight-byte saved pointers and different argument registers.
lessons.solution: The sub reserves 16 bytes. [ebp+8] is the first argument only under this shown prologue and stack-passed convention; do not reuse the offset blindly for optimized or x64 functions.
lessons.task: How many local-space bytes does sub esp,16 reserve?
lessons.hint: The immediate is a byte count.

lessons.title: 32-bit cdecl, stdcall, and fastcall
lessons.body: For common 32-bit cdecl, arguments are pushed right-to-left and the caller removes them. stdcall also commonly uses stack arguments but the callee removes the fixed argument area, often with ret N. Microsoft x86 fastcall passes eligible initial arguments through ecx and edx, with additional arguments on the stack. Naming decoration can help but stripped symbols remove that clue. Infer conventions from both call site and function exit. These keywords do not imply the same stack behavior on Windows x64, whose ordinary ABI uses a unified register-based convention. Variadic functions need special attention because a fixed callee cleanup cannot know an arbitrary argument count.
lessons.code:
push 9
push 4
call add_two
add esp, 8     ; caller removes two 4-byte args: cdecl
; stdcall alternative: callee ends with ret 8

Compile calls.c using the x86 Native Tools prompt and inspect call sites.
Explain the difference between ret and ret 8; the immediate does not include the return address itself.
lessons.solution: This is consistent with cdecl: the caller removes eight argument bytes. eax conventionally carries the int return. Confirm using both caller and callee, not one isolated add.

lessons.title: System V x64: more than two arguments
lessons.body: For ordinary integer/pointer arguments in System V AMD64, the first six register positions are rdi,rsi,rdx,rcx,r8,r9, with the low 32-bit names used for int values. Additional arguments are passed on the stack. Immediately at function entry, before any prologue, the seventh integer argument is at [rsp+8], above the return address. The caller aligns rsp to 16 bytes before call, so the return-address push makes entry rsp eight bytes off that boundary. Floating-point and aggregate classification follows additional rules; do not force every source parameter into this simple integer model. The red zone is a separate System V feature and is not a Windows x64 guarantee.
walkthrough: Use calls.c seven with all arguments distinct.
Break at function entry before the prologue and inspect registers plus x/4gx $rsp.
Step over the prologue and recalculate the seventh argument location relative to the new rsp.
lessons.solution: Before the prologue, [rsp] is the return address and [rsp+8] holds the seventh argument slot. Later stack adjustments change this offset.

lessons.hint: Follow edi, esi, edx, then ecx.

lessons.title: Windows x64: shadow space and stack arguments
lessons.body: Windows x64 passes the first four ordinary integer/pointer argument positions through rcx,rdx,r8,r9. The caller reserves 32 bytes of shadow space even if a callee does not store those registers there. At function entry, [rsp] is the return address, [rsp+8] through [rsp+32] are four home slots, and the fifth argument begins at [rsp+40]. The compiler need not populate home slots, so seeing old values there does not disprove a register argument. Maintain 16-byte stack alignment at ordinary call sites. Floating-point arguments use XMM registers by argument position and have extra variadic rules. Recover the signature using both caller setup and callee use.
lessons.code:
sub rsp, 40   ; common 32-byte shadow area + 8-byte alignment adjustment
mov ecx, 4
mov edx, 9
call add_two
add rsp, 40
ret
walkthrough: Compile calls.c with MSVC /Od /Zi in the x64 prompt.
Inspect seven at entry, especially the fifth, sixth, and seventh stack arguments.
Compare the same function’s Linux GCC layout without assuming shadow space exists there.
lessons.solution: The fifth argument is at entry rsp+40, expressed in decimal bytes. After a prologue, adjust for pushes and local allocation.

lessons.hint: Four eight-byte register home slots.

lessons.title: Saved registers, recursion, and compiler scaffolding
lessons.body: Caller-saved registers may change across a call; callee-saved registers must be restored if used. The sets differ between System V and Windows x64, so consult the ABI instead of transferring every rule. Recursive calls create distinct active frames: a single source local can have several live instances. Tail-call optimization may replace a call/return pair with a jump. Startup routines, security-cookie checks, stack probes, and alignment are compiler/runtime scaffolding, not necessarily original application logic. Establish main’s boundaries and label helpers by evidence; do not erase unfamiliar code just because it looks repetitive.
walkthrough: Trace fact(4) with a frame table n=4,3,2,1.
In GDB stop in the deepest frame; use bt, up, and info args.
Identify which values must survive a recursive call and how they are preserved in the listing.
lessons.solution: fact(4)=24. A register used for the running n cannot simply be assumed unchanged after another call if the ABI makes it volatile. Optimized output may turn recursion into iteration.

lessons.title: Stack arguments without push instructions
lessons.body: A calling convention describes what the callee observes, not one required sequence of instructions. A caller may reserve an outgoing argument area once, then fill it with mov instructions rather than repeatedly pushing. For an ordinary 32-bit stack call, if esp points at argument one immediately before call, the callee entry sees a return address at [esp] and argument one at [esp+4]. Account for call’s own stack effect before interpreting offsets. A push of a scratch register can also reserve a small local slot: its later uses, not the register name alone, reveal the purpose. An extra mov into a scratch register before push may simply materialize a value; assembly output is not fixed by one C spelling. Ordinary mov does not allow both operands to be general memory operands; a register temporary or a specialized string instruction is needed for a memory copy.
lessons.code:
sub esp, 8
mov dword ptr [esp], 6
mov dword ptr [esp+4], 10
call combine
add esp, 8
; At callee entry: [esp+4]=6, [esp+8]=10.
walkthrough: Draw esp before reservation, before call, at callee entry, and after cleanup.
Write an equivalent push-based argument setup for combine(6,10).
Use Godbolt to compare flags and versions; describe equivalence rather than requiring one exact register sequence.
lessons.solution: Equivalent stack argument placement is push 10 followed by push 6, then call. In both versions the first argument is six. A scratch-register push cannot be classified as a saved live value until its restore/use pattern supports that claim.

lessons.body: This function deliberately uses every argument. At n=6 its expression evaluates to 50. On Linux System V x64 the first six integer positions use registers and the last two use stack slots. At entry before a prologue, argument seven is at rsp+8 and eight at rsp+16. After push rbp; mov rbp,rsp, those become rbp+16 and rbp+24. On ordinary x86 cdecl all eight are stack-passed; after a conventional frame prologue they begin at ebp+8 and continue in four-byte increments. Native MSVC x64 instead uses four integer register positions plus shadow space. These offsets belong to the stated observation point, not to every instruction in every build.

lessons.title: Leaf functions, red-zone storage, and misleading offsets
lessons.body: A leaf function does not make another ordinary function call; a nonleaf function does. The System V AMD64 ABI provides a 128-byte red zone below rsp that user-space functions may use for temporary state under its rules. This can explain memory accesses below rsp even when there is no sub rsp instruction. It is not an automatic Windows x64 entitlement, and it should not be generalized to kernel code. Data that must survive a call cannot simply be left in a region the callee is allowed to use. Adding a helper call can therefore change frame allocation and variable placement. Optimizers can also omit rbp as a frame pointer. Recover a stack object from the exact instruction timeline, not from a decompiler label such as local_18 alone; tools may label locations relative to their own frame model.
lessons.code:
Study experiment:
1. Write a leaf that uses a volatile two-element local array.
2. Add a call to a separate noinline helper.
3. Compare GCC x64 -O0 and -O2; then native MSVC x86/x64.
4. Inspect actual rsp movement and live local locations.

Trace rsp at entry, after prologue, around any call, and before return.

lessons.solution: A below-rsp access without explicit allocation can be valid in the relevant System V user-space setting. It is not proof of an invalid frame. On Windows x64 consult its own shadow-space, alignment, and unwind rules instead.

lessons.title: Struct offsets, padding, and alignment
lessons.body: A struct’s field offsets follow alignment rules; summing field widths alone can give the wrong size. On our ordinary GCC/MSVC targets, struct Item {char tag; int count; short code;} commonly has tag at 0, count at 4, code at 8, total size 12. Three padding bytes precede count and two tail bytes make arrays preserve alignment. Packing options can change this, so verify with offsetof and sizeof in a calibration build. During reverse engineering, repeated accesses at +0,+4,+8 with different widths suggest a structure. Do not assign a type solely because one load uses a familiar offset.

Distinguish p->inner.value from p->inner_ptr->value by whether the code loads a pointer before accessing the final field. Ghidra’s decompiler improves after applying supported structure definitions, but an attractive expression is not proof of the type.

lessons.body: A function-pointer table is not a jump table merely because both contain destinations. Here the selected entry is called with a normal argument and returns a value that flows back to the caller. Each table entry is a function pointer; the stride is normally four in these x86 builds and eight in x64. Recover the selector expression and its valid domain. The early negative check makes the remainder an index in zero through two. Observe the computed call target immediately before the call, then verify that its parameter and return follow the platform ABI. Do not infer a C++ virtual method from an ordinary C callback table.

lessons.title: Breakpoint mechanism is separate from its condition
lessons.body: A software execution breakpoint commonly inserts an x86 INT3 byte temporarily; a hardware execution breakpoint uses processor debug facilities without replacing the instruction bytes. Debuggers may show original bytes transparently, so their own dump display is not always a literal view of patched process memory. Hardware resources are limited and target support matters. A condition is a policy for stopping, not a fundamentally separate instruction mechanism: conditions can be associated with supported breakpoint kinds and may be evaluated by the debugger or target. A watchpoint observes a data expression or access, which is different from stopping when an instruction address executes. Choose based on the question you need answered and verify what kind of breakpoint the debugger actually installed.

(gdb) break gate
(gdb) info breakpoints
# Delete the previous breakpoint using its displayed number.
(gdb) hbreak gate
# Conditional example on supported target:
(gdb) break gate if input == 17

lessons.title: PE headers, sections, RVA, and file offsets
lessons.body: PE begins with a DOS header and an offset to the PE signature, followed by COFF and optional headers plus section records. A relative virtual address (RVA) is an address relative to the loaded image base; it is not generally a disk file offset. For bytes backed by a section’s raw data, file offset = RVA - section.VirtualAddress + section.PointerToRawData. The relevant displacement must lie inside the section’s on-disk data. Zero-filled virtual tail bytes may have no corresponding stored bytes. ASLR changes the runtime image base, not the meaning of the RVA. Patch a file using a file offset; set a runtime breakpoint using a virtual address.
lessons.code:
Section VirtualAddress = 0x1000
Section PointerToRawData = 0x400
Target RVA = 0x1234
File offset = 0x1234 - 0x1000 + 0x400 = 0x634
walkthrough: Use dumpbin /headers and Ghidra Memory Map on your local PE.
Locate a string and record RVA, current VA, and raw file offset separately.
Verify the bytes in a hex view before applying a file patch.
lessons.solution: The example offset is 0x634. If the RVA points into zero-filled virtual space beyond SizeOfRawData, this formula does not identify existing file bytes to edit.

lessons.title: Imports, Windows APIs, startup, and strings
lessons.body: Imported functions reveal capabilities, not complete intent. An import of GetModuleHandleA or GetCurrentProcessId is evidence of an API dependency; it does not by itself establish malicious behavior. The Import Address Table contains resolved targets used by indirect calls. Windows programs usually enter runtime startup before main; locate application code using calls and strings rather than renaming entry to main immediately. A-suffixed APIs commonly use narrow strings, W-suffixed variants use UTF-16. UTF-16 ASCII-range text has interleaved zero bytes, so a narrow-string search can miss it. Recover API prototypes to interpret argument order and pointer types correctly.

lessons.title: x64dbg: a practical native debugger workflow
lessons.body: Use x64dbg for a 64-bit PE and its x32dbg companion for a 32-bit PE. Start with your own windows_lab or constructs executable. Opening a program often stops at a system or loader breakpoint before application code; confirm the active module and current instruction. Navigate to application code using module-relative addresses from static analysis and verify the bytes. Set a breakpoint on a chosen instruction, run, then step while observing registers, stack, and dump views. Follow a pointer in Dump to inspect data rather than interpreting its address as the object. Labels and debugger databases are analysis metadata unless you explicitly export a file patch.

Workflow:
1. File → Open your locally built PE.
2. Locate the application module in Modules/Memory Map.
3. Navigate to a verified application instruction.
4. Toggle a breakpoint; run; inspect CPU, Stack, Dump.
5. Step over a call, then repeat using step into.

lessons.body: WinDbg is another native Windows analysis option. Start with a program you built and retain its matching PDB. Launch the executable, establish a breakpoint in your application, and inspect registers, disassembly, stack, and memory. Useful commands include g to continue, p to step over, t to step into, r for registers, k for stack, u for disassembly, db for bytes, and .ecxr for an exception context when one is available. A first-chance exception is a debugger notification before application handling; it is not automatically an unhandled crash. Mismatched symbols can create misleading names and source locations. lessons.title: Windows types, opaque handles, and output parameters
lessons.body: Type names encode contracts but must be checked against definitions. DWORD is a 32-bit unsigned integer even on Windows x64, while SIZE_T scales with pointer width. In Windows LLP64, long remains 32 bits; do not copy a Linux LP64 long layout blindly. A handle identifies a resource according to the relevant API contract; it is generally not an ordinary buffer pointer to dereference. Different APIs use different failure sentinels, so a generic null check is not universally correct. An output parameter passes the address of storage for the callee to fill; its value may change even when the return register only reports success. Recover both channels. A name prefix can suggest a type, but stripped names and misleading names make widths and documented semantics stronger evidence.

lessons.title: First-chance exceptions and application handlers
lessons.body: An exception can create a debugger event before the application has had a chance to handle it. On Windows, a first-chance notification is that earlier opportunity; if application handlers do not resolve the exception, a last-chance notification can occur. A debugger choosing to treat an exception as handled changes the path seen by the application. That can hide its own recovery logic or skip an exception-based control-flow edge. Therefore record both the exception event and what happens when it is delivered according to the intended handler policy. Do not equate every first-chance stop with an unhandled crash. Windows x86 frame-chain conventions and x64 metadata-based unwind/exception handling differ; avoid applying old fixed x86 offsets to x64 code.
lessons.code:
Investigation table:
event → instruction → exception code → handler policy
→ application handler, if any → final observable outcome
A stop is an observation; terminal failure is another observation.
walkthrough: Read the official exception sequence and draw debugger/application hand-offs.
In a program you built, observe a known handled exception only if the local toolchain exercise supplies one; do not execute unknown samples.
Explain how suppressing delivery could invalidate an analysis of application recovery.
lessons.solution: A handled exception can continue normally after a first-chance notification. Marking it handled in the debugger is an intervention, not neutral observation. Last-chance handling is reached only after the earlier handling process did not resolve it.

lessons.title: Read a file-operation call as a typed contract
lessons.body: A call name is only the beginning of API reconstruction. Recover the argument order, handle source, requested operation, result convention, and cleanup path. CreateFile can open an existing file, so its name alone does not prove creation. Its failure sentinel is INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE, not a universal null result. For a simple synchronous ReadFile, the return reports success while an output parameter records the actual number of bytes read; a shorter successful read is possible. Keep buffer capacity, requested count, and actual count separate. If an error must be inspected, capture GetLastError at the relevant point before unrelated calls overwrite the diagnostic state. This lesson’s paper trace is read-only and does not require writing registry or filesystem state.

lessons.title: DLLs and resolved calls: follow the target’s origin
lessons.body: A DLL is a module, not a separate process merely because its code comes from another file. A statically declared import can lead through an import-address slot; a runtime-resolved call can obtain an exported address and store it in a function pointer. GetProcAddress returns an address or null on failure for the requested export. Trace the module handle and exact export name, verify the error path, then follow how the returned pointer is called. A callback reverses the direction of control: your program hands an address to another component, which invokes it later. Missing direct cross-references do not prove the callback never runs. Differentiate module entry routines, exported helpers, and application main; they have different calling and lifetime contracts. Keep this analysis to a harmless local helper when practicing.
lessons.code:
Conceptual control flow:
module handle + exact export name → address lookup
if address is valid → call through matching function-pointer type
otherwise → defined failure path

A function pointer's type must match the actual ABI/signature.

Create a target-origin table with assignment site, possible addresses, call signature, and failure behavior.
Explain why DLL loading alone does not prove a particular export or callback was executed.
lessons.solution: A pointer read from a lookup is evidence of a potential target. An observed indirect call with matching arguments is stronger evidence of actual execution. A DLL’s existence or export table alone does not establish the whole program behavior.

lessons.title: Interpret configuration and network imports conservatively
lessons.body: Windows analysis often includes configuration and communication APIs. A registry query reads a named value; a registry write changes state. Reconstruct the root handle, path, value name, type, buffer length, and result rather than inferring purpose from one import. This course uses only paper traces for these operations. For sockets, distinguish creating an endpoint from connecting it and from sending or receiving data. Requested buffer length is not necessarily the actual transferred count. A receive result of zero can indicate orderly closure for a connection-oriented socket, whereas an error result needs the appropriate API diagnostic. Address-family fields, port byte order, and byte counts matter when reading a structure. Imports show available capabilities; call sites and runtime traces show use. Nothing here requires an external server or a real network connection.

lessons.solution: A byte-stream API can return partial data. Six received bytes do not imply a sixteen-byte message was completed. Imports alone cannot support a complete behavioral verdict; the relevant call sites and data flow must be examined.

lessons.title: Processes, threads, and asynchronous completion
lessons.body: A process provides an address-space/resource context; its threads execute within that context. Creating a worker thread does not imply that the worker has already finished. If a worker is given a pointer to caller-owned data, both the pointer’s lifetime and synchronization must be valid until the worker is done. A thread return value, a creation call’s return handle, and application data written by the worker are separate channels. Follow creation, callback target, argument, wait or completion signaling, and cleanup. A service is an application managed through the operating system’s service infrastructure, not simply any function that runs for a long time. We study these distinctions through local computation and paper traces, not service installation or cross-process manipulation.

start worker with &task
worker computes output=input*2
main waits for worker completion
main reads output, then releases resources

lessons.body: Obfuscation makes behavior harder to understand; optimization makes code efficient and can incidentally look unfamiliar. Neither unusual instructions nor high entropy alone proves deliberate protection. Start with the program’s observable contract: inputs, outputs, external calls, and state changes. Then identify an analysis obstacle, such as encoded strings, indirect dispatch, opaque predicates, or debugger-dependent branches. Compare the protected and plain training builds using the same input set. Keep original bytes and a change log so each simplification can be explained and reversed. All exercises here use the supplied harmless local programs, not unknown downloaded malware.

lessons.body: Timing checks can compare elapsed intervals against a threshold, but scheduling, virtual machines, and normal load can also cause delays. High entropy, unusual sections, and a small import set are hints, not definitive tests. Distinguish an encoded data buffer from restored executable code. A memory dump is not automatically a runnable PE: imports, relocations, entry state, and permissions may need reconstruction. lessons.title: Source auditing: trace untrusted data to operations
lessons.body: Auditing follows input through parsing, validation, arithmetic, allocation, indexing, and output. Write each object’s capacity and each index’s valid interval. Check negative inputs, truncation, multiplication overflow, and signed/unsigned conversions before memory access. A check performed after a load does not protect that load. Validate a declared length against both available input and destination capacity. Use strtol-style parsing with error and range checks when converting text; atoi cannot report errors distinctly. A warning-free build is useful but does not prove memory safety. Translate suspicious assembly back to the same constraints you would check in source.

lessons.title: Memory corruption and exploitation: what a crash does not prove
lessons.body: An out-of-bounds access can disclose adjacent data, overwrite state, or crash, depending on operation and layout. A stack overwrite can affect local data and, in some circumstances, control data; a crash alone does not demonstrate control-flow execution. Understand the distinction between reachability, primitive, impact, and reliability. Stack canaries detect some overwrites; NX/DEP restricts execution from data pages; ASLR changes addresses; PIE supports relocating executable code; control-flow protections constrain some indirect transfers. These defenses reduce or detect classes of exploitation but do not repair the source bug. The exercises keep protections enabled and study a supplied local array-index defect, then fix it and validate the repair.

Root cause: index used without complete bounds validation.

lessons.title: Sanitizers: reproduce, diagnose, repair, regress
lessons.body: AddressSanitizer instruments many memory accesses and reports problems such as buffer overflows. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer checks selected undefined operations. Instrumentation changes binary layout and timing, so use it to diagnose source-level training programs while retaining ordinary binaries for reverse-engineering comparison. Read the error category, access size, call stack, and object bounds; do not stop at the first printed line. Reproduce with the smallest input, fix the root cause, rerun the reproducer, then run a broader valid/invalid input set. No report means no detected issue on those executions, not universal safety.

lessons.title: Fuzzing: a bounded harness and useful corpus
lessons.body: A fuzzer repeatedly exercises a target with generated or mutated inputs. A harness defines the callable boundary, data model, and reset behavior. Seed inputs should cover ordinary valid cases and interesting edges, including empty input, minimal length, maximum allowed length, and inconsistent length fields. Coverage-guided fuzzing uses execution feedback to explore new paths; it still cannot guarantee all paths. A crash needs reproduction and minimization, and many crashing inputs may share one root cause. Our standard-library Python harness enumerates a bounded index set and records sanitizer exits; it is a smoke fuzzer, not coverage-guided. LLVM libFuzzer is an optional next step with a dedicated byte-buffer entry point.

diagnostic.prompt: C: int xs[3]={2,4,6}; int total=0; for(int i=0;i<3;i++) total+=xs[i]; What is total?
diagnostic.explain: The loop visits indexes 0,1,2; the total is 2+4+6.

diagnostic.prompt: Little-endian: bytes 34 12 represent a 16-bit unsigned value. Write the hexadecimal value with a 0x prefix.
diagnostic.explain: The low byte is stored first, so the value is 0x1234.

diagnostic.prompt: Intel syntax: mov eax, [rdi+8] loads data or computes only an address? Answer data or address.
diagnostic.explain: Square brackets request a memory load. lea computes an effective address.

diagnostic.prompt: After cmp eax, ebx, which branch tests signed less-than: jl or jb?
diagnostic.explain: jl uses signed comparison flags; jb tests unsigned below.

diagnostic.prompt: Windows x64: which register carries the first 32-bit int argument?
diagnostic.explain: The Windows x64 first integer argument uses RCX, or ECX for a 32-bit int. Linux System V differs.

diagnostic.prompt: In GDB, which command sets a breakpoint at main?
diagnostic.explain: break main (or b main) sets a breakpoint; run starts the process.
